editorial:
The Adventures of Tarzan is a 15-chapter silent serial produced by Great Western Producing Company and distributed by Numa Pictures Corporation, with its first chapter released December 1, 1921. Elmo Lincoln, who originated the screen Tarzan in the 1918 Tarzan of the Apes, makes his third and final appearance in the role; the screenplay draws from two Burroughs novels, The Return of Tarzan (1913/1915) and Tarzan and the Jewels of Opar (1916/1918). The complete 15-chapter cut has not survived â€” what circulates descends from a 10-chapter 1928 re-release, with surviving elements held at the UCLA Film and Television Archive and the Niles Essanay Silent Film Archive. The Film Detective issued a transfer from 35mm archival elements in August 2022 as part of its Tarzan Vault Collection Blu-ray.

For a creator, the print and both Burroughs source novels are in the US public domain by term expiry. The live trap is the TARZANÂ® trademark (USPTO Reg. 5498007), which Edgar Rice Burroughs, Inc. actively enforces against commercial projects using the character's name and likeness regardless of copyright status â€” ERBI has a documented history of pursuing trademark claims even after Burroughs copyrights lapsed. A documentary or archival presentation screening the silent footage carries lower risk; any commercial product titled with or trading on the Tarzan brand requires trademark clearance from ERBI before release.
faq: Can I use this film in a commercial project?

The print is in the US public domain by term expiry, and so are the underlying Burroughs source novels. The operative constraint is trademark: TARZANÂ® (USPTO Reg. 5498007) is actively held by Edgar Rice Burroughs, Inc. and covers film and entertainment products. Using the Tarzan name or character commercially requires trademark clearance from ERBI even though the copyright has expired.
Is the Film Detective Blu-ray safe to copy?

No. The Film Detective's 2022 restoration from 35mm archival elements is a new copyrighted work â€” their specific transfer and any newly recorded score are protected even though the underlying 1921 film is not. The Archive.org copies above provide PD-safe access to the underlying footage.
